board_fact: White's queen stands on d4 with no black pawn touching it, and Qf6 would have covered d4.
lesson: When an enemy piece parks in the middle, look first for a move that attacks it.

board_fact: The g8 knight goes to the rim and has to move again to g4, while the f8 bishop and king are still at home.
lesson: Choose the square your knight really wants before you move it; moving the same piece twice gives the other side a free move.

board_fact: The queen leaves d1 on move 6 and Black's c8 bishop can come to g4 to hit it, which h3 would have prevented.
lesson: Bring the queen out only when it has a job, or it will be pushed around while they develop.

board_fact: On move 2 nothing is settled in the middle, and d4 would have covered c5 and e5.
lesson: Play in the middle of the board in the first few moves; edge pawn moves can wait.

board_fact: White answers with Kc1 and the bishop goes back to d7 two moves later.
lesson: A check they simply step away from costs you a move; only check when it gains something.

board_fact: The e-pawn is stopped by Black's pawn on e5 and has no moves left, and d7-d5 can come and hit it.
lesson: Don't push a pawn to a square where it is frozen and an enemy pawn can attack it.

board_fact: The queen takes f6 from the g8 knight and is back on d8 one move later, with c7 and the c8 bishop losing a guard.
lesson: Develop knights and bishops before the queen; a queen that comes straight home has lost you a move.

board_fact: The b1 knight's square is c3 and the pawn takes it, while Nc3 would have covered b5, d5 and e4.
lesson: Before pushing a pawn, check whether a knight or bishop wanted that square.

board_fact: The queen gives up c6, where it had 20 moves, for a square with 9.
lesson: Keep your strongest piece where it sees the most squares; drifting to the edge halves its power.

board_fact: The knight takes c3, the square White's c-pawn needs to keep Black out of d4, and the knight has to move on to e2.
lesson: Don't put a knight on the square your own pawn needs; the pawn is what keeps enemy knights out.

board_fact: Black answers d6 and the bishop's diagonal from a3 is shut, while e5 would have taken f6 from Black's knight.
lesson: A centre pawn push that takes squares from their pieces usually beats a bishop move they can block.

board_fact: White's knight on d5 and bishop on c4 are both untouched by a pawn, and c6 would have hit the knight.
lesson: A knight planted in your half is the first thing to chase away.

board_fact: The bishop steps back from f4 and stops watching Black's pawn on g5, while Qg6+ would have covered f5, f6, f7, g5, g7, g8 and h5 around the king.
lesson: When your pieces already crowd their king, keep adding to it; a quiet retreat hands them time to get organised.

board_fact: The h2 pawn can come to h3 and hit the bishop, which is back on c8 next move.
lesson: Before putting a bishop beside their king, check whether a pawn can simply push and chase it home.

board_fact: The knight comes back from d4 to f3, while from f5 it would have watched d6, e7, g7 and h6, with Black's bishop on d6 untouched by any pawn.
lesson: Don't pull a knight back from a strong central square while it still has good work to do forward.

board_fact: The b1 knight starts a three-move trip to d2, f1 and g3, and moves again at once, while d4 drops to two guards with one attacker.
lesson: A knight that needs three moves to find a job is three moves the other side can use.

board_fact: Black meets the check by walking the king to d7 and on to c8, losing castling, while Rf7 would have blocked on f7.
lesson: If a check can be blocked by a piece, block it; walking the king out of its shelter costs you more.

board_fact: The knight goes back to b1 with two moves left instead of six, and e4 drops to one guard with Black's knight on f6 watching it.
lesson: Retreating a piece to the back row usually makes it the weakest thing on the board.

board_fact: From f3 the knight would have covered d4 and e5, the squares Black's pawn on e5 and bishop on c5 use; from c3 it covers neither.
lesson: Develop toward the middle: the knight that touches the central squares is worth more than the one that does not.

board_fact: In this line Black plays h6 and White's knight on g5 is driven to h3 and then g1, while Qe2 would have covered f3 for it.
lesson: If one of your pieces is about to be chased, give it a good square to go to before you develop elsewhere.

board_fact: The knight leaves d7 with one guard fewer and White's knight comes to d6, a square no black pawn can ever attack.
lesson: Before a natural knight move, ask which square it stops guarding; a knight landing in your camp is hard to remove.

board_fact: The king on e7 was one of two guards of d6, and after it steps away d6 has one guard left with White's knight on e4 hitting it.
lesson: Count what your king is guarding before you move it; in the late middlegame the king is a real defender.

board_fact: Black's bishops and the b8 knight are still at home, and White's c4 pawn can push to c5 to hit the pawn on b6.
lesson: Get a piece out on every opening move you can; a quiet pawn move just hands them a target.

board_fact: Black's f8 bishop and king have not moved, and Bd6 would have developed and allowed castling.
lesson: Finish getting your pieces out and your king castled before you start lining up rooks.

board_fact: White's pawn on e4 holds the centre and nothing of Black's touches it, while f5 would have hit it.
lesson: Strike at the pawn that holds their centre together instead of making another quiet piece move.

board_fact: White plays Bf4, which hits d6, and the queen has to move again to e6.
lesson: Put your queen where their pieces cannot reach it; every time it is chased they develop for free.

board_fact: The pawn takes f6 from the g8 knight, and White's e4 pawn can push to e5 to hit it.
lesson: Keep f6 free for your knight; a pawn there blocks your own development and loosens your king.

board_fact: Black's pawn on e6 can come to e5 and hit the bishop, which ends up on g5 in this line anyway.
lesson: Check for a pawn that can push and hit your bishop before you place it.

board_fact: The queen drops from 17 squares to 11, White's g-pawn can come to g4 to hit it, and it ends up on g6.
lesson: An early queen looks active but is really a target; bring it home and develop instead.

board_fact: The pawn takes f3 and e2 from White's bishop on h5, which drops from six squares to four.
lesson: Don't push a pawn onto the square your own bishop wants to use.

board_fact: White's f1 bishop and b1 knight have never moved and the king is still on d1, while Black's queen walks in to b2 in this line.
lesson: Get your last pieces out before you move the ones that are already working.

board_fact: The queen takes f6 from the g8 knight and has to move again to b6, and c7 and the c8 bishop lose their guard.
lesson: The queen belongs behind the other pieces in the opening, not in front of them.

board_fact: On move 2 no white pawn is in the middle, d4 would have covered c5 and e5, and b7-b5 can come and hit the bishop.
lesson: Put a centre pawn out first; a bishop placed before the centre can be pushed around.

board_fact: White's e4 pawn can push to e5 and hit the knight, which in this line is driven from f6 to e5 to g6 and back to g8.
lesson: If a pawn can push and kick your knight, the knight is not really developed.

board_fact: White's knights on e4 and e3 sit in the middle with no black pawn touching them, and f5 would have hit the one on e4.
lesson: Use a pawn to push an enemy knight out of the centre; pawns do that job better than pieces.

board_fact: The knight goes back to b8 with two moves instead of five, and d8, c8, e7 and a7 each lose a guard.
lesson: Never undevelop a piece without a reason; you hand over two moves for nothing.

board_fact: White answers c3, the queen's squares drop from 19 to 16, and the b2 pawn can later come to b4 to hit it.
lesson: A check they answer with a move they wanted to play anyway helps them, not you.

board_fact: The bishop stands in front of White's unmoved pawn on d2, while Nf3 would have covered d4 and e5.
lesson: Don't park a bishop in front of your own unmoved pawn; the pawn and the bishop both get stuck.

board_fact: The king stays on d2 while Kd3 would have covered c2, c3, c4, d4, e2, e3 and e4, and the bishop moves again to g7 anyway.
lesson: In an endgame the king is a fighting piece; walk it toward the middle before you fiddle with other pieces.

board_fact: No pawn of either side is on the d-file, and Rd1 would have covered d2 up to d8; castling leaves the file to Black.
lesson: When a file has no pawns on it, grab it with a rook before they do.

board_fact: White's pawn on e4 is unchallenged and d5 would have hit it and opened the c8 bishop.
lesson: Castling is good, but if your pawn can challenge their centre right now, that often comes first.

board_fact: Once the c-pawn goes past c3, no white pawn can ever cover d4, and Black's knight comes there.
lesson: Every pawn push leaves a square behind it that no pawn can guard again; check which square before you push.

board_fact: White's h2 pawn comes to h3 and hits the knight, and Black has to spend h5 just to hold it there.
lesson: A knight on g4 that a pawn can push at is only visiting; holding it there costs you more moves.

board_fact: Nothing is developed yet, and Nf3 would have covered d4 and e5, which the g-pawn move touches neither of.
lesson: Use your early moves to bring pieces out, not to arrange pawns.

board_fact: The d-pawn could have gone to d5 and taken c6 and e6 from Black's knight; after the knight move Black settles with Nf6 and e6.
lesson: When a centre pawn push takes squares from their pieces, take the space.

board_fact: White's b2 pawn can come to b4 and hit the knight, which drops from eight squares to six and then goes to d7.
lesson: A knight is only well placed if a pawn cannot chase it off.

board_fact: White's knight on e5 and bishops on f4 and c4 all sit with no black pawn touching them, and b5 would have hit the one on c4.
lesson: With three enemy pieces aimed at your king, hit one of them with a pawn rather than adding another defender.

board_fact: White's queen sits on d7 inside Black's camp where no pawn can reach it, and Rad8 would have attacked it; instead d3-d4 can hit the queen.
lesson: When their queen is sitting in your position, attack it; driving it out is worth more than your own queen trip.

board_fact: White just plays Kb1, and in this line the rook reaches d6 and the knight c7, squares no black pawn can ever attack.
lesson: A check that only nudges their king is a free move for them; improve your worst piece instead.

board_fact: White's queen stands on d4 with no black pawn touching it, Nc6 would have hit it, and the g4 pawn can come to g5 to hit h6.
lesson: Develop with a move that also attacks something; a knight to c6 gets a piece out and asks the queen a question.

board_fact: The b-pawn move touches nothing in the middle, while d4 would have covered c5 and e5.
lesson: Fight for the two big central squares before arranging pawns on the wing.

board_fact: Black's bishop on g4 has no white pawn touching it and h3 would have hit it; instead Black's d6 pawn can come to d5 and hit the bishop on c4.
lesson: When their bishop pesters you from g4, a simple h3 asks it a question; do that before placing your own bishop.

board_fact: Black's king, both bishops and the g8 knight are all at home, and Nf6 would have developed and covered d5 and e4.
lesson: Spend opening moves getting pieces out; a rook's-pawn move does not.

board_fact: After the two-square push no black pawn can ever attack White's knight on g5, while h6 would have hit it at once.
lesson: Push a pawn one square when that attacks their piece; two squares can mean you never get to attack it.

board_fact: The bishop drops from six squares to one, shut in by White's own pawns on g4 and h3.
lesson: Count a bishop's squares before you place it; a bishop behind your own pawns does nothing.

board_fact: Black's knight sits on d4 with no white pawn touching it, c3 would have hit it, and b7-b5 can come and hit the bishop on c4.
lesson: Kick the enemy knight out of the middle with a pawn before you improve your own pieces.

board_fact: Black's knight on d5 has no white pawn touching it, and c4 would have hit it.
lesson: Chase a knight off its central square while you still can; castling can wait a move.

board_fact: Both moves develop the same c8 bishop and no measured fact separates them; I cannot tell why e6 is worse than g4.
lesson: Not clear from this position.

board_fact: Black's b8 knight and c8 bishop are still at home, White's a2 pawn can come to a4 to hit the pawn on b5, and the pawn then goes on to b4.
lesson: Flank pawn pushes before your pieces are out only give the other side targets.

board_fact: Black's king and both bishops have not moved while White's queen sits on d4, and Be7 would have developed and allowed castling.
lesson: Get a bishop out and the king castled before you touch the queenside pawns.

board_fact: Black's h7 pawn can come to h6 and hit the bishop, while from e3 it would have guarded d4.
lesson: Place a bishop where a pawn cannot push at it, especially when it has a job holding the centre.

board_fact: The pawn move opens White's c1 bishop and no measured fact counts against it; the engine's queen move is a direct attack rather than a better square.
lesson: Not clear from this position.

board_fact: White plays Nd5, which hits f6, and the queen is back on d8 next move, with a8 and c7 left unguarded.
lesson: Before the queen steps out, check whether a knight can jump to a square that hits it.

board_fact: The queen takes d2, the only free square of White's unmoved c1 bishop, which then has no moves at all.
lesson: Don't put your queen on the one square your undeveloped bishop needs to get out.

board_fact: Kc4 would have covered b3, b4, b5, c3, c5, d3, d4 and d5, while the pawn move puts a pawn where f5-f4 can hit it.
lesson: In a pawn endgame march the king forward first; pawn moves on the wing can only create targets.

board_fact: Every black piece except the queen is on its starting square, and White's d4 pawn can push to d5 to hit the pawn on c6.
lesson: Bring out a knight before you make small pawn moves; a pawn move can be attacked, a knight is harder to send home.

board_fact: The rook leaves a7 with no guard at all while White's queen on b7 attacks it, and the rook has to move again to b6.
lesson: Before you move a rook off its file, check what it was the only defender of.

board_fact: The queen comes out on move 5 and is back on d1 by the end of this line, and the f3 knight, d2 and the c1 bishop each lose a guard.
lesson: If your queen's trip ends back on its starting square, that was a lost move; develop a piece instead.

board_fact: The knight goes to the edge and is back on b1 next move, while Bg2 would have covered f1, f3, h1 and h3.
lesson: A knight on the edge reaches fewer squares; work out its real square before you move it.

board_fact: Black's f7 pawn can come to f6 and hit the knight, which goes on to g4, and d4 is left with no guard.
lesson: A knight deep in their camp is only strong if their pawns cannot push it away.

board_fact: The bishop moves a second time, to a square Black's b7 pawn can hit by coming to b5, while a3 would have covered b4 next to Black's queen on a5.
lesson: Moving the same bishop again to a square a pawn can hit wastes the move twice over.

board_fact: White's g2 pawn can come to g3 and hit the queen, and g7 and the f5 bishop each lose a guard, while f6 would have hit the pawn on e5.
lesson: Check for a pawn that can push at your queen before you move it to the edge.

board_fact: White plays Ne1 and the bishop drops back to e6 next move, with b7 left unguarded.
lesson: If a bishop has to come back two moves later, the first move was the mistake; place it where it can stay.

board_fact: No white pawn is in the middle yet, d4 would have covered c5 and e5, and b7-b5 can come and hit the bishop.
lesson: Put a pawn in the centre early; a bishop out before the centre pawns can be pushed around.

board_fact: The b-pawn was the only guard of c6, which now has none, and White's a2 pawn can come to a4 to hit the pawn on b5.
lesson: When all your pieces are out, improve the worst one; a wing pawn push only leaves holes behind it.

board_fact: White's own pawn on e4 and Black's on e5 block the e-file, so the rook looks at nothing, while Qd2 would have covered b4, c3, f4, g5 and h6.
lesson: A rook on a file blocked by pawns is doing no work; put it where the file can open.

board_fact: Black plays h6 and the bishop is on f4 next move, and the f7 pawn can also come to f6 to hit g5.
lesson: A bishop a pawn can push at has not developed; it will be sent back and the move is gone.

board_fact: The rook leaves f1, so f2 drops from two guards to one with Black's bishop on c5 aiming at it.
lesson: A rook beside your king is often a defender; check what it is holding before you move it.

board_fact: Blocking the check on g6 leaves the knight with no moves at all, and f7 drops to two guards with one attacker.
lesson: When you block a check, make sure the blocking piece still has somewhere to go.

board_fact: The f-pawn move empties f7, so Qh5+ comes at once and the king has to step to d8 and give up castling.
lesson: Moving the pawn in front of your uncastled king opens a line straight to it; castle first.

board_fact: The knight went to the a-file edge with 3 moves instead of 7, and b5 is one move from hitting it.
lesson: A knight at the side of the board does less, and one pawn push can send it back.

board_fact: The knight gave up e5, where it had 8 moves and no white pawn can ever reach it, and the line walks it straight back to e5.
lesson: If your piece stands on a square no enemy pawn can attack, leave it there.

board_fact: The queen took f3 with the knight still sitting on g1, and the line has to move her on to g3.
lesson: Do not park your queen on a square your own knight needs.

board_fact: The pawn advanced while the knight was still on b1, and Nbd2 would have brought that last piece out.
lesson: Finish bringing your pieces out before you push pawns up the board.

board_fact: The rook dropped back to b7 and the line then plays Rb4 anyway, while e5 is left with one defender and one attacker.
lesson: If you play a move one turn later anyway, the move in between was a free turn for your opponent.

board_fact: The knight's moves fall from 7 to 1, and it now stands between the queen on d8 and the rook on f8.
lesson: Pulling a piece back to your own back row usually takes away its own moves.

board_fact: White's knight goes to c7 next move, where it hits the bishop on e6, and Na6 was the move that watched c7.
lesson: Watch the square an enemy piece wants to jump to, even when your own move looks more active.

board_fact: The h2 pawn was the only thing guarding the queen on g3, and after the push she has no defender at all.
lesson: Before you push a pawn, check whether it is the only guard of one of your pieces.

board_fact: White's g- and h-pawns are ready to run, and the line goes g4, g5, h4, h5 straight at the king's new corner.
lesson: Look at where the opponent's pawns are heading before you decide which side to castle.

board_fact: Black's knight lands on e4, a square no white pawn can ever attack, and Nbd2 was the move that covered e4.
lesson: Cover the square an enemy knight is heading for before you make quiet pawn moves.

board_fact: The queen stopped guarding g5, which now has one defender and one attacker, and left a8 with none.
lesson: When you move your queen, check which of your own squares she was holding together.

board_fact: The queen stopped guarding c7, which white's bishop on g3 already looks at down the diagonal.
lesson: Count the defenders of the pawns near your king before you move the piece that holds them.

board_fact: The pawn stopped one square short: from f4 it would attack the black pawn on e5 and cover g5.
lesson: A pawn move that touches the opponent's centre pawns is worth more than one that only shuffles.

board_fact: The bishop's moves fall from 9 to 6 and b4 is one move from hitting it, while from e5 it would face the knight on d4.
lesson: Put your bishop where a pawn cannot push it away.

board_fact: White's bishop on f4 has no black pawn attacking it, and Bd6 would have faced it down the same diagonal.
lesson: An enemy bishop on a strong square should be met or traded, not walked around.

board_fact: The rook left f1, so the f2 pawn drops from two defenders to one, and black's bishop comes to h4 to look at it.
lesson: Before you move a rook, see what it was quietly guarding.

board_fact: Black answers the check with Rd6, and e7-e5 is one move from kicking the bishop away.
lesson: A check the opponent answers with a move they wanted anyway just gives them a free turn.

board_fact: The king is still on e8 with the rooks apart, and after Qf5 the line castles long two moves later.
lesson: Get your king out of the middle before you shuffle your queen around.

board_fact: Nothing of white's touches the black rook on b5, and a4 would attack it, while the bishop goes where h5 can kick it.
lesson: Deal with an enemy rook that has got into your half before improving a quiet piece.

board_fact: Black's a5 pawn is free to come to a4 and hit the knight on b3, and white's own a4 would have frozen that pawn for good.
lesson: Stop the pawn that is coming to push your piece away before it gets there.

board_fact: White blocks with Be3 and the queen has to go back to f6 next move.
lesson: A check that only makes the opponent place a piece where it wants to be costs you a move.

board_fact: The pawn shuts the c8 bishop's diagonal: that bishop had five squares and now has one.
lesson: Do not block your own bishop in with a pawn before you have given it a way out.

board_fact: a6 is one move from hitting the bishop, and the line ends with it back on e2.
lesson: Do not place a bishop where a single pawn move sends it home again.

board_fact: White's knights on e4 and e3 have no black pawn attacking them, and f5 would have hit the one on e4.
lesson: A pawn is the cheapest way to chase a knight out of your half.

board_fact: Three black pieces sit unchallenged on c5, g4 and f2 and the knight's moves rise from 2 to 6, so I cannot tell why rescuing it is worse than Qd2.
lesson: When a move looks natural and the engine still dislikes it, say so instead of inventing a reason.

board_fact: The queen was the only guard of d4 and c2, and after she leaves, c2 has an attacker on g6 and no defender.
lesson: Count what your queen is holding before you move her across the board.

board_fact: The bishop on d3 still blocks the d2 pawn, which has no move at all, and Bc2 would have freed it.
lesson: Move the piece that is standing in front of your own pawn before you do anything else.

board_fact: The rook left the h-file, so the h6 pawn now has black's rook on h7 attacking it and no defender.
lesson: A pawn deep in enemy ground needs its guard; do not step away with a check instead.

board_fact: f5 is one move from hitting the queen, and the knight on c3 loses a guard as she goes.
lesson: Keep your queen off squares a pawn can reach, or she will spend the game running.

board_fact: White just steps to c1 and the queen moves on to b3 next.
lesson: Checks that the opponent answers with a normal move only lose you time.

board_fact: The knight gave up d4, which no white pawn can ever attack, for a square g4 can hit.
lesson: Never swap a square no pawn can reach for one a pawn can push you off.

board_fact: The king walked off h8 and h7, so the rook on h8 is left with no defender and the h7 pawn with one.
lesson: Count what your king is guarding before you walk it to another square.

board_fact: b4 is one move from hitting the bishop, and the line puts it on e7 the very next move.
lesson: If a pawn can chase your bishop, go straight to the square you will end up on.

board_fact: White's rook sits on d6 with nothing attacking it, and Ke7 would have attacked it.
lesson: With the queens gone your king is a fighting piece, so use it to chase an intruder.

board_fact: Black's knight on c5 has no white pawn attacking it, and d4 would have hit it, while the bishop goes to d2 and then on to e3.
lesson: Hit the enemy knight that has settled in your half instead of shuffling a bishop.

board_fact: The bishop's moves fall from 6 to 4 and the queen on e2 loses a defender.
lesson: Tucking a bishop back for safety often leaves it looking at nothing.

board_fact: The knight's moves fall from 6 to 4 on the edge, and the d7 pawn loses a defender.
lesson: A knight on the edge of the board covers half as much as one in the middle.

board_fact: Black's queen sits on a5 untouched, and a3 would let the b3 pawn come to b4 and hit her with the a-pawn holding it.
lesson: When the enemy queen comes out early, gain time by preparing a pawn that attacks her.

board_fact: White blocks with c3, which also attacks the bishop, and the bishop goes to d6 next move.
lesson: A check your opponent blocks with a move they wanted anyway loses you a turn.

board_fact: White's queen on g6 and bishop on f4 can never be hit by a black pawn, and Qf7 would have faced the queen.
lesson: When an enemy queen settles next to your king, challenge it instead of hunting pawns.

board_fact: Black's knight on d4 has no pawn attacking it, and the knight took c3, the square white's c2 pawn needed to hit it.
lesson: Leave the pawn's square free when a pawn is the piece that should do the chasing.

board_fact: f5 is one move from hitting the knight, and the line pushes it on to g3.
lesson: A knight that a pawn can hit is not placed, it is only visiting.

board_fact: The bishop's moves fall from 7 to 3 and the line walks it on to f7.
lesson: A bishop in the corner of the board sees very little; give it open lines.

board_fact: The queen took f3 with the knight still on g1, and Bg4 drives her on to g3.
lesson: Keep f3 free for your knight; the queen there invites a bishop to chase her.

board_fact: The f-pawn's advance gives up e3 for good, and black's bishop takes that square next to white's king.
lesson: Once a pawn goes past a square, nothing can guard it again, so check what you are giving up.

board_fact: The knight's moves fall from 5 to 2, and f8, h7 and d7 each lose a defender.
lesson: Retreating a knight to the back row undoes the development you already did.

board_fact: White's bishop on c4 has no black pawn attacking it, and Na5 would have hit it.
lesson: Push the enemy bishop that is aiming at your king away before you settle your king.

board_fact: The bishop's moves fall from 9 to 5 on the edge of the board.
lesson: Count the squares a piece will have on its new home before you send it there.

board_fact: a3 is one move from hitting the bishop, and e5 drops to one defender with an attacker on it.
lesson: A bishop that a pawn can chase gains you nothing and loosens what it left behind.

board_fact: The king stepped to a square f4 can push it off again, and from c4 it would attack the c5 pawn.
lesson: In pawn endings walk your king towards the pawns that will decide the game.

board_fact: Black's king is still on e8 and the line never castles, while g4 is one move from hitting the advanced h-pawn.
lesson: Castle before you start pushing pawns on the wing.

board_fact: The king steps to e2 and then to f1 next move anyway.
lesson: When your king has to step aside, go to the square you actually want it on.

board_fact: The knight gave up d4, which no white pawn can ever attack, for a square g4 can hit, and the line brings it back to d4.
lesson: A square no pawn can attack is worth keeping; moving off it just wastes moves.

board_fact: c3 is one move from hitting the knight, and the line sends it back to c6.
lesson: Check for the pawn that chases you before you jump a knight forward.

board_fact: The bishop has one move in the corner and the line brings it back to b7.
lesson: A piece in the corner has almost nothing to do; keep it where it has squares.

board_fact: The g-pawn's advance stops guarding f6 and h6, and white's bishop goes to e7, a square no black pawn can reach.
lesson: A pawn that advances gives up the squares it used to guard behind it.

board_fact: The king shuffles to the corner while the knight is still on b1, and the line brings the king back to g1.
lesson: Bring your last pieces out before you make small king moves.

board_fact: The queen gains squares, from 13 to 16, and only f2 and g2 lose a defender with no attacker on them, so I cannot say why Ng3 is better.
lesson: If the board does not show a reason, do not make one up.

board_fact: The queen's moves fall from 23 to 13, and the line has to move her again to b2.

lesson: Look along your own bishop's diagonal before you put a rook on it.

board_fact: Blocking the check on f2 leaves the rook with no legal moves at all.
lesson: Blocking a check can bury the blocking piece, so see whether the king can just step aside.

board_fact: The bishop gives up c4 and its moves fall from eleven to seven, while the rook on f5 loses two.
lesson: Before moving a well-placed piece, count its moves on both squares.

board_fact: The king is pushed on to c7 two plies later, and the b7 pawn is left with no defender.
lesson: When your king must move, choose the square it will not have to leave again next move.

board_fact: The bishop lands on its own rook's file: the rook on e1 drops from nine moves to six.
lesson: Check your own rook's file before you place a piece on it.

board_fact: Black's g7 pawn can come to g5 and hit the bishop, and the bishop also freezes its own f3 pawn.
lesson: A bishop placed in front of their pawns can be pushed away, and the move you wanted will still be there.

board_fact: The king leaves d5 and walks away from Black's king on g5 and the g7 and h6 pawns.
lesson: March your endgame king toward their pawns, because distance from the action is a lost move.

board_fact: The bishop moves on to g3 two plies later, and meanwhile its own e4 pawn has no move at all.
lesson: If the piece has to come back, the first move was not worth playing.

board_fact: White's f2 pawn can step to f4 and hit the knight, whose moves have already dropped from eight to three.
lesson: A knight that lands where a pawn can hit it loses both the square and the time.

board_fact: The king step costs it a move, four down to three, and the king goes on to g3 at ply 6 anyway.
lesson: A waiting king move while your rook sits passive is a move given away.

board_fact: The d4 pawn stops covering c5 and e5, and Black's bishop walks to f4, d6 and then c5.
lesson: When you push a pawn, the squares it used to cover become their squares.

board_fact: The bishop checks, the king steps to c7, and the bishop is back on f4 two plies later.
lesson: Before a check, ask what it changes; if the answer is nothing, you have lost a move.

board_fact: Bf5, the engine's move, is played anyway two plies later, by which time Black's f-pawn has moved.
lesson: Place the piece where it must go first, because pawn moves can wait.

board_fact: The b5 pawn was the one stopping a3-a4, and White plays a4 at once; c4 also loses a defender.
lesson: A pawn that is holding back their pawn should usually stay where it is.

board_fact: The pawn takes the square its own king needed: the king on f4 drops from two moves to one, and Kg5 comes at ply 4 anyway.
lesson: Do not put a pawn on the square your king has to use.

board_fact: The packet lists the played move and the engine's move as the same move, Kf6, with identical follow-up lines, yet reports a 54cp loss.
The check only sends the king to c3, and the bishop's moves fall from nine to seven before it retreats to f8 at ply 4.
lesson: A check that improves nothing costs you both the move and the square.

board_fact: The knight on a4 was the queen's only guard on b2, and it left.
lesson: Ask what a piece is protecting before you send it somewhere more exciting.

board_fact: White's g2 pawn can come to g4 and hit it, and Rhe8 was played anyway two plies later.
lesson: A pawn push their pawn can meet head-on just wastes the move.

board_fact: From d1 the queen no longer guards a4, which White attacks twice and Black now defends once; from a1 she still would.
lesson: When you have a choice of checking squares, pick the one that keeps doing your other jobs.

board_fact: The king comes back to f6 two plies later, after White's pawn has already gone to d5.
lesson: In a pawn race, a king move you have to undo costs you the race.

board_fact: The rook gives up the seventh rank behind the b6 and h6 pawns, and its king loses a square as well.
lesson: A rook behind their pawns does far more than a rook tucked in beside your king.

board_fact: The check only sends the king to h1, and the knight stops guarding e6, f7 and h7.
lesson: A knight covering squares near your king is worth more there than one spare check.

board_fact: The check sends White's king to e4, the active square it wanted anyway, and the rook's moves fall from ten to eight.
lesson: A check that pushes their king toward where it wants to go is helping them.

board_fact: With the rook on c1 instead of the open a-file, Black's rook settles on a3 where no white pawn can reach it.
lesson: If they own the open file, meet them on it, or they walk in behind your pawns.

board_fact: The king steps back to the second rank, leaving the d4 pawn with one defender and the rook on e2 with none.
lesson: In a rook endgame your king belongs in front of your pawn, not behind it.

board_fact: The f7 pawn was e6's only defender, and after the push e6 has none.
lesson: Pawns can never move back, so check what yours is defending before you push it.

board_fact: The b6 pawn stops covering a5 and c5, and White's rook checks from c5.
lesson: A pawn push gives up the squares it used to cover, so look for the check that opens.

board_fact: On a3 the king lines up with the e7 bishop, so the b4 pawn has no move at all, and b3 is played anyway at ply 4.
lesson: Keep your king off the diagonal your own pawn needs to move along.

board_fact: The bishop steps onto the sixth rank in front of its own rook, which falls from twelve moves to seven.
lesson: Keep your rook's rank clear, because a bishop parked on it costs the rook half its reach.
